title: Four Foundations of Mindfulness, Part 2: Observation of Actions
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: The talk emphasizes the importance of cultivating mindfulness and presence in daily life, encouraging listeners to pay attention to their bodies and be fully engaged with the world around them. By doing so, we can develop a sense of connection and intimacy with others and with ourselves, and find ways to contribute positively to the world. This practice is not about achieving some grand state of enlightenment, but rather about being present and helpful in our daily activities, using techniques such as zazen and ritual language to stay grounded and aware.

Someone run the lights up to the max, I forgot my reading glasses.
I don't know if there's much more available.
Oh yeah, there we go.
So I want to open and close tonight's talk with a short poem by Naomi Shihab Nye, different ones.
This one's called "Famous."
I think it's a good poem about one aspect of our bodhisattva ideal: the ideal of the bodhisattva to be a being that helps everyone wake up.
And it doesn't necessarily have to be a flashy deal.
It can be pretty quiet.
*The river is famous to the fish.
The loud voice is famous to silence, which knew it would inherit the earth before anybody said so.
The cat sleeping on the fence is famous to the birds watching him from the birdhouse.*
*The tear is famous, briefly, to the cheek.

The boot is famous to the earth, more famous than the dress shoe, which is famous only to floors.
The bent photograph is famous to the one who carries it, and not at all famous to the one who is pictured.
I want to be famous to shuffling men who smile while crossing streets, sticky children in grocery lines, famous as the ones who smile back.
I want to be famous in the way a pulley is famous, or a buttonhole.
Not because it did anything spectacular, but because it never forgot what it could do.
I want to be famous to shuffling men who smile while crossing streets, sticky children in grocery lines, famous as the ones who smile back.

We do need our smarts, and we need our mind, and we need our thinking, and we need our knowledge of history, and our concern about what's coming, or what might be.
But by staying connected to our body, we also keep some of our eye on the ball of what is now, what's the feeling of this moment.

Remember that part?
He said, just contemplate that you have a body.
Let me get the exact line for you.
*Just to be observing the process of coming and going in the body, and the process of dissolution in the body, things are always changing in the body.
And both the process of coming to be, and the process of dissolution, and just being mindful of the fact, there is a body here.
There is a body here.* Not that the body that's here always feels good, or bad exactly, but our embodiment is our presence.
It's our here-ness.
It's our place on the earth.
We are made out of earth stuff.
And so now he's going to suggest that we pay attention to the body through all of our activities, through all of our activities.
*Moreover, when the practitioner is going forward or backward, she applies full awareness to her going forward and backward.
When she looks in front or looks behind, bends down or stands up, he also applies full awareness to what he's doing.
He applies full awareness to wearing the Sangati robe or carrying the alms bowl.
When he eats or drinks, chews or savors the food, he applies full awareness to all this.
When passing excrement or urinating, he applies full awareness to this.

So let's remember to notice what we're actually feeling and doing, moment to moment.
Because the body is the only vehicle we have, right?

The only way that we can practice, the only way that we can help, the only way that we can find our way, whether we perceive the world to be in crisis or perceive the world to be okay or some of both or neither.
And that was part of how Blanche Hartman practiced.
She had a very body-centered practice.
I always see that she was really paying attention to how she moved around in space.
And so her book jumped off my shelf again, so I want to share a few more little snippets from Blanche, the collection of Blanche's words called *Seeds for a Boundless Life*.
I think they're really in accord with this recommendation from the Buddha to notice the body through all of its changes, through everything that happens, to be right here, to be right here.
And maybe that's a lot of what we do on Wednesday night and have done at least once a week for nearly 25 years.
Just be here together, just be here together.
And so this little part was entitled by the editor [unclear: "Earthlin"], "Being Just This One, Being Just This One."
Blanche said, *I'll read you this quotation from Dogen Zenji's fascicle called Self-Receiving, Self-Employing Awareness,* [unclear: "foreign"] Japanese Bendowa.
*He says, The zazen of even one person at one moment imperceptibly accords with all things and fully resonates through all time.
The zazen of even one person at one moment imperceptibly accords with all things and fully resonates through all time.*
*He is saying that our present practice will affect all time, past, present, and future.
Our practice affects the past, too.
And each moment of zazen is full of this realization.
We're not only practicing by sitting, but also before and after we sit.
This kind of practice fills the universe.
It would be tragic if practice ended after 40 minutes of sitting.
Therefore, we cannot measure our practice through time or space.
We can't really measure our personal practice.

Dogen says, Know that even if all Buddhas in the ten directions, as numerable as the sands of the Ganges, exert their strength and with Buddha's wisdom try to measure the merit of just one person's zazen,* so zazen's seated meditation, *if all those Buddhas try to measure the merit of one person's zazen, they will not be able to comprehend it.

The spirit of our practice is to practice without trying to acquire anything or accomplish anything because we already have everything we need, without trying to be anything other than just this one, because just this one, just this one, is a Buddha from the beginning.
We practice to express and realize and settle on the suchness of this one.
We practice to express, to realize and settle on the suchness of this one so that it can manifest in whatever activity we undertake.
So it can manifest in whatever we do.
So that our oneness with all things becomes evident.
Can we do it?
Can we make it happen?
Just sit.
Just be willing to be here as this one and allow what arises to come out.
Be willing to be just this one.
Can we just sit zazen?
I'm not judging whether we're doing it right or doing it wrong.*
Just practice knowing the body.
Just practice knowing the body.

One of the ways that Thich Nhat Hanh recommends, and that Blanche also is going to recommend in this little part called "Re-energizing Life," is it does help us to use language to have little sayings for ourselves.
And so we use language in a ritual way here, right?
Little chants, and a little chant before the talk and so on.
But she's going to suggest to us that we have some little verses that we say at pivotal parts of the day.
And Thich Nhat Hanh talks about that too, and he has a whole book of them actually.
I'll see if I have it.
So anyway, this is Blanche again.
*In our practice we re-energize life each month by renewing our vows on the day of the full moon in the Bodhisattva ceremony.* Which we do not quite on the full moon, but we do that.
*Every day our liturgy begins with the three refuges.
These are also verses one can use in daily activity.* Sorry, *there are also verses one can use in daily activity.
For example, the verse for waking up in the morning:*
*This morning, as I wake, I vow with all beings to see each thing as it is and not to forsake the world.*
It's interesting, huh?
*This morning as I wake, I vow with all beings to see each thing as it is and not to forsake the world.* Not to forsake the world, so that sounds kind of political, doesn't it?
Not to give up.
Not to forsake.
And of course, how do we know if we're seeing things as it is, right?
Hard to know.
So I see things not as worse than they are, not as better than they are, as they are.
There's also a verse for bathing.

*As I bathe this body, I vow with all beings to wash this body free from dust, healthy and clean, within and without.* And I don't remember about the waking up verse, but I remember they had that bathing verse by the showers and stuff at the Zen centers.
And she says, *For home leavers there's a verse for shaving the head:*
*Now I am being shaved.
May I with all beings cut off selfish desires.*
Cut them off.
Cut off the selfish desires.

*There's a verse for offering incense, a verse for brushing the teeth, for washing the face, and of course a whole extended ritual for receiving food,* which we do, and we will do next week at Rohatsu.
*In short, there are vows.
There are vows for all the activities of our daily life to remind us that our activities of body, speech and mind are not just for us.
They're to benefit all beings.* And finally at the end of the day, like the end of the day trying to benefit all beings all day, at the end of the day we say:
*This evening as I sleep I vow with all beings to still all things and to put an end to confusion.*
*This evening as I sleep I vow with all beings to still all things and put an end to confusion.* So if we really can set it down, maybe in some way confusion stills, at least for the night.
It's ready to come back in the morning.
It's for the night.
It can still.
Last section.

I remember that on the application for Tassajara Zen Mountain Center practice periods, and this is very topical because a couple of our colleagues were just admitted to go to Tassajara for the next practice period: Ewan McGee, maybe you know Ewan, and Susan Elby in Vancouver, and our own Elizabeth McDonald is trying to go back there too.
She's been there a bunch of times.
I wonder what they think of her.
I'm sure they appreciate when she comes back.
I remember that on that application years ago we used to have a quote from Suzuki Roshi.
Quote, *students should be as intimate as milk and water.
Students should be as intimate as milk and water.*
More intimate than that actually, because we're all living Buddha's life as our own.
What Suzuki Roshi was pointing to was that we support and depend on each other.
We make the practice period what it is.
We make the practice period what it is.
We make that.
And if we want to develop an intimate sangha where we feel completely supported by each other and where we recognize that our practice is supporting everybody, we can do that.
It's up to us.
I can't emphasize strongly enough how important a difference in our lives that kind of mutual support and intimacy can make.

When we speak of the three treasures, we speak of the treasure of Buddha, of the teacher, of someone who sees and understands how we need to live in this life and tells us of the Dharma, the teaching that he gave us, and of the sangha, the community of practitioners.
These are the three jewels of our practice.
One of the ways we develop this kind of intimacy is by practicing closely together.
We sit long periods together, creating a very bonding experience.
To make our wholehearted effort in the company of others who are also making their wholehearted effort is really very unifying, even if nothing is happening.
Even if nothing is happening, it's worth the effort.
We can make an effort to develop intimacy within Zen training periods.
My late husband, Liu, called the tight quarters of Zen practice potato practice.
He said, if you dig a bunch of potatoes out of the ground, they all have dirt on them.
But you don't pick up each potato and scrub it separately.
You put them in a bucket with some water and you stir them around and they bump into each other and they clean each other up.
Or if you've ever had a rock tumbler or polished stones, you put the stones in a cylinder, you add some water and abrasives, and you just let the stones tumble over and over and over on the rollers.
They keep falling on top of each other, smoothing each other off.
Pretty soon you have polished stones.
That's how polished pebbles are made.
That's how Zen practitioners bond: by being in close proximity, living together and learning together about human life.
So we do that.
We don't live together full time, but we live together a little, a bit here and a bit there, and it adds up.
And we always are together, in a way, anyway.
We're always together.
One of the ways in which Zen practice is through initiating a head student called the shuso in the practice period.
The shuso helps to create this bonding.
The shuso is sort of like an elder sibling for all the other monks.
The shuso's job is to model what it is to be a wholehearted practicing monk.

Shusos set the tone for us and they support everyone else in following the schedule completely, first and foremost, by doing it themselves, by energetically engaging in all the activities of the practice.
The shuso awakens before everyone else and rings the wake-up bell.
The shuso cleans the bathrooms, so as not to get a big head.
Or at some practice centers, takes care of the compost and the garbage and the cleaning of the compost buckets.
The main role of the shuso is to set an example of real engagement and to develop an intimate relationship with everyone in the practice period.
To further build intimacy with the students, the shuso has tea, one on one, with everyone in the practice period, which is a three month long Zen training, to get to know each student.

The shuso is also invited to teach by giving dharma talks, and at the end of the practice period there's a ceremony in which each student in the practice period asks the shuso a personal question about practice.
By that time, after sitting off and on and engaging together for months, the life inquiries are expected to come from the heart, to be serious questions about life.
The shuso responds to each person who is asking the question, not to the words but to the person who is asking, not to the words with which the question is expressed but to the heart of the question.
The most important thing for the shusos is to be completely authentic and be willing to reveal their life as it is.
To be completely seen in order to be seen completely.
In order to be willing to be seen as they are, shusos must be willing to be as they are.
You have to learn to really appreciate this particular Buddha, the shuso who is now sitting in the dharma seat giving his or her heart to help the students practice.
So that's what we've got on our agenda: to have our winter practice period starting in January, early in January.
We're working on getting all the details written up and so on.
And we'll go through the first week of March, which is actually a couple weeks longer than some of our other winter practice periods have been.
It's about 8 weeks; usually it's around 6.
We decided we needed more time in the tumbler to get more shiny.
And we do have a shuso.
Maybe you know that Kate Ryushin, Kate is going to be our shuso.
We've had maybe 8 or 9 shuso here over the decades, and this is the third one I think that I've supported as teacher.

So it's 100%.
Probably the other 6, that I was less directly involved in hearing how they were feeling about it, told Norman the same thing.
Probably didn't feel ready.
But that's how we know they're ready.
That's how we know.
Kate will support us in the way that Blanche is describing here, by just being yourself and by being willing to be in the bucket, being willing to be in the rock tumbler with us.
And for those 8 weeks I hope that we will make an extra effort to show up for a life in the way that's right for us, the gentle, kind way to show up for ourselves and show up for each other.
And there's something else I was going to say but I didn't write it down.
I guess it's just that we talk about things like beginning this greed, hate and delusion, the 3 root poisons in the human mind of anger, confusion or ignorance and greed and desire.
It's actually true.
It's actually a real thing.
So our practice is not to shy away from any of this.
There's more to this than just having some nice friends and a quiet room to sit together in.
So it's wonderful that Kate's topic is going to be communication and conflict.
How did she know that would be so topical?
She thought about this a while ago.
So I hope we really get to study that together in a real way, and for each of us to find out how am I going to bring this out to my world and my life.
My hope from the national challenge of our political scene is that we'll each have to find out how we're going to be famous.
Are we going to be famous in an ordinary quiet way?
Famous like a buttonhole or a pulley?
Will we be famous in a more spectacular way, talked about on Facebook as the one who bravely did this thing or that thing?

It turns out it's really expensive to stay in D.C. around the inauguration.
The prices go way up, like ten times normal.
So they're challenged by that.
But they're sleeping five to a bunk in some Airbnb somewhere.
Tried Trump's hotel last week.
No, it's booked out.
But anyway, several Zen women, our Zen women colleagues, are going to be part of the Million Women March the morning after, the day after the inauguration.
There's going to be a big one in Seattle though that we can all go.
Oh good, we can go to Seattle.
Good.
In Bellingham too?
Oh good.
Good.
Is that right?
Well, maybe we can include a walk through downtown in our sesshin.
Our practice period has a one day sesshin towards the beginning to really settle in.
So maybe part of our settling is to walk together with our Zen paraphernalia.
Maybe I'll have the staff.
Yeah?
Yeah, we'll find out.
So we'll include that somehow, for those who want to go.
And we can have people who stay and sit, right?
Famous like buttonholes and famous like marchers.
So anyway, I hope that on the one hand we all can find what's my way to contribute, and on the other hand, we can let that be enough.
One of the things that I love about our practice is that we recognize that culturally or just humanly, we're good at a couple of different things, usually by default.
We're good at being sort of busy and intense.
Riled up, yeah.
And we're good at collapse and avoidance, and a certain kind of rest.
But practice helps us to learn to be good at relaxed and alert.
And those don't usually go together in our culture.
So we do need to be alert, I think.
We do need to be paying attention.
No matter what your political views, none of us can hide under a rock for four years or eight years and just come out after that.
But it's no good to be upset the whole time.
Maybe there's anger that keeps us going, but it's no good to be so consumed by anger that we can't hardly function.
Maybe we can do just enough.
Find out what just enough is.
And maybe it's a little more than we're comfortable with.
You may need to be uncomfortable.
I think it would be a great contribution of ours to the whole conversation to model and live in our bodies: alert, determined, motivated, and relaxed, and kind, and willing to stay connected to love.
Which brings me to the closing poem of another Naomi Shihab Nye, which I'm sure I've read before, called "Shoulders."
*A man crosses the street in rain, stepping gently, looking two times north, two times south, because his son is asleep on his shoulder.
No car must splash him, no car drive too near to his shadow.
This man carries the world's most sensitive cargo, but he's not marked.
Nowhere does his jacket say fragile, handle with care.
His ear fills up with breathing.
He hears the hum of a boy's dream deep inside him.*
We're not going to be able to live in this world if we're not willing to do what he's doing with one another.
*The road will only be wide and the rain would never stop falling.*
*A man crosses the street in rain, stepping gently, looking two times north and south, because his son is asleep on his shoulder.
No car must splash him, no car drive too near to his shadow.
This man carries the world's most sensitive cargo, but he's not marked.
Nowhere does his jacket say fragile, handle with care.
His heart, his ear and his heart fills up with breathing, and he hears the hum of a boy's dream deep inside him.*
We're not going to be able to live in this world if we're not willing to do what he's doing with one another.
*The road will only be wide and the rain will never stop falling.*
And the "with one another" needs to actually include everybody, not just the people that we agree with or that we like, or where's it going to end?
Thanks as always for being here and for participating in the ritual of giving and receiving a talk that we can only do together.
